narration.text: You heard that right. The first child ever born has just killed the second, out in a field, with no one watching.
Cain thought the ground would keep his secret. It did not. The earth itself cried out.
So how does a man go from bringing God a gift to killing his own brother? And what will God do with him now?
I keep the old stories. Tonight I will tell you one about two brothers.
Stay to the end, because this same story hides a man who never died.
And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD.
Think of what that meant to her. The woman who lost a garden is holding a son, and she calls him a gift.
And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
In the old language, Abel's name sounds like a breath, a vapour, something gone in a moment. Hold on to that.
Two brothers, two kinds of work. One followed the flock across the hills. The other bent his back over the hard soil his father had been told about, the ground that would bring forth thorns.
Nothing in the text says either job was better. A shepherd and a farmer, side by side, just outside the gate of Eden. Both of them were needed.
And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD.
And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof.
Notice the small words. Cain brought some fruit. Abel brought the firstlings, and the fat, the very best he had, before he kept anything for himself.
And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering: But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.
We are not told how they knew. Perhaps the smoke of one altar rose straight to heaven, and the other drifted and died in the wind. However it happened, both brothers saw it.
And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.
His face fell. You know that look. It is the face of someone who wanted the reward without giving the heart.
And here is the part most people skip. Before anything terrible happens, God goes looking for Cain, and He speaks to him like a father.
And the LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen? If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted?
It is not a threat. It is an open door. Cain can still turn around.
And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.
Sin crouches at his door like a hungry animal. Cain can master it. The question is whether he will.
And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.
That is all the text gives us. One sentence. No struggle described, no cry for help. Just a field, and then one brother instead of two.
Abel never speaks a single word in the whole story. The only voice he is given is his blood, crying from the ground.
And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
Listen to that answer. First a lie, and then a joke. Am I supposed to look after him? He keeps the sheep, not me.
But God already knows. The question was never for information. It was one more chance to tell the truth, and Cain lets it pass.
When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.
Do you see the shape of it? The man who loved the ground is cut off from the ground. The thing he worked for most will not answer him any more.
Even now he does not say he is sorry. He says it hurts. He is afraid someone will do to him what he did to Abel.
And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.
And this is the surprise. God judges Cain, and then God protects him. Mercy, even here, for the man who shed the first blood.
And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.
Nod means wandering. The man told he would wander settles in a land named for it.
Remember that he walked out from God's presence. Because the rest of this story is about two ways to live: walking away from God, and walking with Him.
And Cain knew his wife; and she conceived, and bare Enoch: and he builded a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch.
Keep that name in mind, Enoch. There are two men called Enoch in these chapters, and they could not be more different. One is remembered for a settlement, the other for a walk.
Cain's family grows fast, and so does everything they make. Herds and tents, harps and pipes, tools of bronze and iron. Clever, gifted, restless people.
And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
But listen to the man at the end of that line, Lamech, speaking to his two wives.
for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt.
If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.
He turns God's mercy into a boast. Cain killed and was afraid. Lamech kills and sings about it.
In just a few generations, violence has become a song. And the song is getting louder.
Meanwhile, far from that camp, Adam and Eve are still grieving the son they lost. They have buried one child, and the other is gone east.
And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.
And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.
So now there are two families on the earth. One builds and boasts. The other calls on the name of the LORD. Same parents, same world, two very different directions.
And then the Bible slows down into a list. Names, ages, sons and daughters, and the same three words again and again.
And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.
And he died. Seth lived, and he died. Enos, and he died. Like a bell tolling across the generations, every few verses. You almost stop hearing it.
Read this chapter slowly and it starts to feel heavy. Every life, however long, ends the same way. Until one does not.
And Enoch lived sixty and five years, and begat Methuselah:
And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years, and begat sons and daughters:
This is the other Enoch. Not the boy a murderer named his settlement after, but a quiet man from Seth's family line. No settlement, no song, no weapon. Just a man and his God.
Notice when it starts. After his son is born. Something about holding that child turned him toward God, and he never turned back.
Walked with God. Not once, not only on a special day. Three hundred years of ordinary mornings, side by side, in a world that was walking the other way.
And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years:
And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.
No and he died. Just and he was not. For one man, the bell stops ringing.
Cain walked away from God. Enoch walked with God until God simply took him home.
And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died.
Enoch's son outlives everyone in the Bible. But the world around his tent is getting darker every year. What happens when almost no one walks with God any more?
A few more generations pass, and a father in Seth's line names his boy with a sigh and a hope.
And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.
Comfort from the cursed ground. Do you hear the echo? It is Cain's ground, still hard, still thorny, still waiting for comfort.
And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.
Some read those hundred and twenty years as a shorter life, and some as a countdown. Either way, God is still waiting.
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
Not some thoughts. Every one. Only evil. All day long. What began in one field has spread to every tent on the plain.
And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.
Read that again. It grieved Him at His heart. This is not an angry machine. This is a Father whose children broke His heart.
But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.
One man. In a whole world gone wrong, one man. Who was he, and what would God ask him to do?
Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.
There it is again. Walked with God, the same words as Enoch.
The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.
And then God speaks to him, in a world that has forgotten how to listen.
Imagine hearing that, alone on a dry hill, with the noise of a violent world below you. And then being told to build. Not to fight back. To build.
Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch.
But with thee will I establish my covenant; and thou shalt come into the ark, thou, and thy sons, and thy wife, and thy sons' wives with thee.
Hear the mercy inside the judgment. Before a single drop falls, God makes a promise and leaves a door open.
No rain has fallen anywhere in the story so far. No one has ever seen a flood. Noah picks up his tools anyway.
Day after day the beams go up on dry ground, while the neighbours watch and laugh and wonder what is wrong with the old man.
Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.
And of every living thing of all flesh, two of every sort shalt thou bring into the ark, to keep them alive with thee;
Two of every kind, and food for all of them. God is not only ending a world. He is carrying one through.
That is what walking with God looks like when the whole world is shouting. You just keep doing the next thing He told you, one beam at a time.
Here is what most readers miss in these chapters full of names and deaths.
Cain and Enoch are not just two men. They are two ways to live, and everyone in this story is on one of them.
Cain's way starts with a gift given without the heart, and it ends with a lonely man who walks out from God's presence, into the land of wandering.
Enoch's way has no great deeds at all. No battle, no miracle. Just a man who kept walking beside God, one ordinary day after another.
Lamech's song was loud. Enoch's walk was quiet. God took Enoch.
Abel's life was a breath, gone in a moment. Yet his gift is the very first one the Bible says God accepted.
And notice who God goes after first. Not Abel. Cain. Before the murder He warns him, and after it He marks him to keep him alive.
And then Noah, at the very end, is the proof that Enoch's way never died out. Even in the worst generation, one man was still walking it.
God does not wait for you to become Enoch before He comes looking for you.
These chapters leave you with one simple question. Which way are you walking today?
Tell me in the comments: which brother, or which Enoch, do you see in yourself?
Next, the rain begins and the flood comes. Watch the next story with me.
